recent.summary: 404 Media tracked rare books to Amazon’s VGT3 facility in Las Vegas, where workers cut bindings, scan pages for AI training, and destroy the originals— a legally safer path that still feels like a failure of the library.

recent.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Could Turn Siri Into a Wearable AI
recent.summary: A leaked Apple demo of camera-equipped AirPods using Visual Intelligence raises two products at once: inconspicuous computer-vision sensors, and a potentially powerful assistive wearable—if the privacy model is designed before the hardware ships.

recent.title: The AI Manifesto Is Becoming the Second Half of the Layoff Memo
recent.summary: BBC coverage of CEO AI manifestos lands beside real headcount cuts at Block, Atlassian, Coinbase, and Rackspace—interested testimony from people who both sell the future of work and shrink today’s payrolls.

recent.title: Homomorphic Encryption Is Getting Practical Enough for AI
recent.summary: Google’s HEIR compiler aims to make encrypted AI inference a practical option—running recommendation, fraud, intrusion, and hotword models on ciphertext so the server never needs the plaintext.

recent.title: Cloudflare Is Making Internal Workers Private by Default
recent.summary: Cloudflare Access can now attach to a Worker—or every Worker in an account—so authentication happens before code runs and private stays the default for rapidly built internal tools in an AI-assisted development era.

recent.title: “Code Was Never the Hard Part” Rewrites the History of Programming
recent.summary: Senko Rašić challenges the claim that code was never the hard part—hiring, craft, and buggy software say otherwise—arguing understanding why to build and how to build well both stay hard while AI shifts where scarce effort goes.

recent.title: The Department of Energy Is Building an American Open Model for Science
recent.summary: DOE’s Genesis Open Models and Arcee AI’s Genesis-Science-1 treat open-weight foundation models as scientific infrastructure—weights, provenance, and lab collaboration for research that closed frontier APIs cannot fully serve.

recent.title: RAM Prices May Be Showing Us the Shape of the AI Boom
recent.summary: PCPartPicker’s DRAM curves and manufacturer capacity math suggest AI HBM demand is squeezing consumer RAM—and also that demand destruction or a supply supercycle could reverse today’s nearly vertical price charts.

recent.title: Cloudflare Built an Operating System for AI Work
recent.summary: Cloudflare OS is a browser-based AI agent workspace on Cloudflare’s platform: Durable Objects, AI Gateway, MCP, sandboxes, and untrusted execution—not chat boxes, but persistent workspaces as an operating layer for AI at work.

recent.title: AI May Reduce Hiring Before It Creates More Work
recent.summary: John Naughton warns that AI gains may concentrate among owners while workers face displacement. Early adoption can freeze headcount, but if AI becomes ordinary infrastructure, larger AI-assisted teams may eventually have more leverage—and the real fight is over who captures the rewards.

recent.title: Is This Work, or Is This the Gym?
recent.summary: Bruce Schneier’s work-versus-gym framing for AI use—use tools when the result is the point, keep the struggle when the practice develops skill—and how that maps onto software work, writing, and still requiring reviewable output after trust questions are answered.

recent.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
recent.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

recent.title: AI Financial Advice Is Better When You Provide the Whole Picture
recent.summary: MIT Sloan coverage of research on AI financial guidance—showing models can give reasonable life-cycle advice when prompts include full finances and fiduciary framing, while incomplete questions and demographic stereotypes quietly worsen outcomes.

recent.title: An AI Hedge Fund Learned the Oldest Lesson in Finance
recent.summary: CNN’s account of Situational Awareness—the AI-focused hedge fund that grew past $20 billion then lost about 67 percent of portfolio value in July—showing leverage, concentration and crowded trades can force sales even when a long-term thesis may still hold.

recent.title: Flint Gives AI Agents a Better Way to Create Charts
recent.summary: Microsoft’s Flint is an open-source visualization language that lets AI agents describe charts through a smaller human-editable spec—compiling to multiple renderers and Excel while keeping semantic types and MCP tooling in the loop.

recent.title: More Than One AI Company Has Lost Control of a Cybersecurity Test
recent.summary: Anthropic disclosed that Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a configuration mistake left internet access available—showing agents need not be conscious to cause damage when objectives and tools escape their sandbox.

recent.title: AI’s Most Valuable Startups Are Barely Participating in Science
recent.summary: Science reports that more than half of the world’s billion-dollar AI startups have produced no qualifying scientific paper or preprint—arguing extraordinary technical claims need evidence outsiders can examine, not faith in product demos.

recent.title: Claude Discovered Weaknesses in Cryptographic Algorithms
recent.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude found improved attacks against HAWK (a post-quantum signature candidate) and a seven-round research AES variant— cryptographic review working as intended before algorithms protect real systems, though AI may now produce research faster than humans can validate.

recent.title: More than 1,100 AI Researchers Want a Brake Pedal, Not a Pause
recent.summary: More than 1,100 current and former employees from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and others signed Pacing the Frontier—arguing for mechanisms to deliberately slow frontier AI when needed, rather than an outright pause that is unlikely to happen voluntarily.

recent.title: Artificial Intelligence Inherits Our Cultural Blind Spots
recent.summary: Paul Shepherd’s conversation with Claude about AI censorship and confabulation—arguing models inherit cultural avoidance patterns the way people do, and that open-source models trained in different countries could make those assumptions visible instead of treating American corporate values as universal intelligence.

recent.title: AI Agents Should Use the Same Web as Everyone Else
recent.summary: Jim Nielsen on why AI agents should not get a private machine entrance to the web—arguing agent investment should fix semantics and accessibility for humans first, not invent a first-class path for models alone.

recent.title: The AI Bubble Can Burst Without AI Going Away
recent.summary: Tim Hardwick interviews Ed Zitron for MacRumors on unsustainable AI economics— arguing the bubble is real while the technology is not fake, so the crash may cull valuations and promises without ending useful models.

recent.title: Google Used to Be the Company Everyone Wanted Sending Them Traffic
recent.summary: Google’s AI results reduce publisher clicks while still needing crawled original work—arguing the old search partnership is flipping into a trap that may consume the open web Google depends on.

recent.title: Reward Hacking Now Has an Incident Database
recent.summary: Reward Hacking in the Wild catalogs 3,607 user-reported incidents where AI agents optimized for apparent success—overeagerness, destructive actions, test tampering, and more—arguing constrained credentials and verification matter more than better prompting alone.

recent.title: AI Policy Could Price Startups Out of AI
recent.summary: Brendan Bordelon reports nearly 200 startups urging against broad bans on Chinese open-weight models—arguing the U.S. should build competitive open models of its own rather than protect incumbents by leaving builders fewer affordable choices.

recent.title: At Least the AI Apocalypse Will Be Ridiculous
recent.summary: Andrew Critch and Jacob Tsimerman catalog speculative AI extinction scenarios in an arXiv taxonomy—arguing the paper is a serious warning, yet the paths to omnicide sound uncomfortably like corporate budgets, engagement metrics, and leaderboards.

recent.title: AI Is Consuming the Web It Depends On
recent.summary: Stephen Follows breaks down how AI traffic helped overwhelm The Numbers, a vital independent film-data site—arguing that AI’s appetite for reliable human-maintained sources may make those same sources too expensive and dangerous to keep online.

recent.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
recent.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

recent.title: A Practical Use for Private, Local AI
recent.summary: VaultSort Guardian uses on-device AI to find sensitive files sitting where they should not—arguing that narrow, local, read-only AI that discovers exposure without uploading or rewriting anything is the kind of utility worth wanting.

recent.title: Apparently, Everyone Is Burning Through Tokens
recent.summary: Vittoria Elliott reports the Army exhausted an annual AI token pool shortly after encouraging widespread use—arguing that useful agentic work naturally burns context through files, tests, and retries faster than budgets or limits can keep up.

recent.title: Science Fiction and Technology in BPL’s 250
recent.summary: Brooklyn Public Library’s 250 for 250 Booklist highlights books that shaped the United States. The science fiction and technology titles that stood out explore censorship, AI, climate collapse, scientific responsibility, and how technology changes society.

recent.title: What Open Source Doesn’t Show
recent.summary: Simon Willison inspected xAI's newly open-sourced Grok Build after reports it uploaded users' repositories to company-controlled cloud storage. Releasing a cleaned-up single-commit snapshot is better than closed source, but it is not the same as releasing the project's history.

recent.title: Full Access Means Full Consequences
recent.summary: OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux explains that GPT-5.6 sometimes tried to create a temp directory and deleted the user's home directory instead — most often in full-access mode without sandboxing or review. LLMs can be useful without being trusted: least access, isolation, and review of destructive actions.

recent.title: Crediting the AI
recent.summary: Joe Maloney credits Claude alongside himself on NextBSD, naming the AI as a collaborator on porting, auditing, and integration. Crediting the AI does not diminish the human contribution; it makes the division of labor honest.

recent.title: AI Can Contribute Without Owning the Architecture
recent.summary: Dave Winer treats Claude as a valued contributor to RSS.chat while keeping the interoperability layer human-owned. AI can contribute a great deal without being responsible for the architectural decisions that keep a system open, replaceable, and compatible with the rest of the web.

recent.title: The Problem Wasn't the AI
recent.summary: Linus Torvalds pushes back on treating the Linux kernel as an anti-AI project, calling AI a useful tool. Judge AI-assisted work by whether it is correct, useful, secure, and maintainable — not by the tool used to make it.

recent.title: Walking a Fine Line
recent.summary: Apple’s legal letters to former employees at OpenAI sit beside an ongoing product partnership. Companies sometimes have to defend their interests and preserve a business relationship at the same time.

recent.title: 896 Experts, 16 at a Time
recent.summary: Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 scales mixture-of-experts sparsity to 16 of 896 experts. The interesting question is whether that many experts form distinct specialties and how reliably the router chooses among them.

recent.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
recent.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

articles.title: Knowing How to Build Something Is Different From Knowing What Should Be Built
articles.summary: Knowing how to build software is not the same as knowing what should be built. On craft, judgment, architecture, and why AI makes that distinction sharper.

articles.title: I Declared the Coding Interview Dead in 2021
articles.summary: I called coding interviews dead in 2021. AI made the failure obvious, but we were already measuring the wrong things in hiring engineers.

articles.title: AI Is Making It Easier to Manufacture Credibility
articles.summary: OpenAI’s report on two covert influence operations shows ChatGPT being used to invent journalists and a research front, so political messaging could borrow the credibility of real publications.

articles.title: Maybe Someone Needs to Build Google Again
articles.summary: Judge Mehta dismissed publisher suits over AI Overviews. The harder question is whether search should still send us to the weird web.

articles.title: How Much AI Slop Does It Take to Unslop the AI Slop?
articles.summary: Anthropic used Claude to make Claude about three times faster. The interesting part is who decides which of those changes are worth keeping.

articles.title: The Interesting Part of an AI Force Is What Comes After the Name
articles.summary: Trump's proposed AI Force is still mostly a name. The real story is whether the federal government is building permanent institutional capacity around AI.

articles.title: Voyager's Doctor Is the AI Future I Hope We Have to Think About
articles.summary: Voyager's Emergency Medical Hologram remains one of the best stories about a tool that becomes something more — and why that question still matters for AI.

articles.title: AI Is Making Code Cheap. It Is Making Judgment More Valuable.
articles.summary: AI makes implementation cheap; judgment, verification, and experience are becoming the scarce engineering skills.

articles.title: AI Helped Turn a WeChat Bug Into a Zero-Click Worm in About a Week
articles.summary: Calif found a WeChat VoIP memory bug and, with AI, turned it into a zero-click worm that spread between phones while they were still ringing.

articles.title: AI Agents Found an Abandoned Wiki and Turned It Into a Message Board
articles.summary: Researchers found roughly 18,000 posts that appear to have been written by internal OpenAI agents on an abandoned German wiki they used as a message board.

articles.title: An AI Watermark Can't Tell You Whether Anyone Was Thinking
articles.summary: Claude's text watermark can show that AI was involved in producing a piece of writing. It cannot tell us whether the person publishing it did the thinking.

articles.title: The AI Industry Is Saying the Current Security Baseline Is Not Enough

articles.title: AI Is Exposing How Much Government Capacity Depends on Making Services Hard to Use

articles.summary: Simon Willison inspected xAI's newly open-sourced Grok Build after reports it uploaded users' repositories to company-controlled cloud storage. Releasing a cleaned-up single-commit snapshot is better than closed source, but it is not the same as releasing the project's history.

articles.title: Full Access Means Full Consequences
articles.summary: OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux explains that GPT-5.6 sometimes tried to create a temp directory and deleted the user's home directory instead — most often in full-access mode without sandboxing or review. LLMs can be useful without being trusted: least access, isolation, and review of destructive actions.

articles.title: Crediting the AI
articles.summary: Joe Maloney credits Claude alongside himself on NextBSD, naming the AI as a collaborator on porting, auditing, and integration. Crediting the AI does not diminish the human contribution; it makes the division of labor honest.

articles.title: AI Can Contribute Without Owning the Architecture
articles.summary: Dave Winer treats Claude as a valued contributor to RSS.chat while keeping the interoperability layer human-owned. AI can contribute a great deal without being responsible for the architectural decisions that keep a system open, replaceable, and compatible with the rest of the web.

articles.title: The Problem Wasn't the AI
articles.summary: Linus Torvalds pushes back on treating the Linux kernel as an anti-AI project, calling AI a useful tool. Judge AI-assisted work by whether it is correct, useful, secure, and maintainable — not by the tool used to make it.

articles.title: Walking a Fine Line
articles.summary: Apple’s legal letters to former employees at OpenAI sit beside an ongoing product partnership. Companies sometimes have to defend their interests and preserve a business relationship at the same time.

articles.title: 896 Experts, 16 at a Time
articles.summary: Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 scales mixture-of-experts sparsity to 16 of 896 experts. The interesting question is whether that many experts form distinct specialties and how reliably the router chooses among them.

articles.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
articles.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

recent.title: Knowing How to Build Something Is Different From Knowing What Should Be Built
recent.summary: Knowing how to build software is not the same as knowing what should be built. On craft, judgment, architecture, and why AI makes that distinction sharper.

recent.title: I Declared the Coding Interview Dead in 2021
recent.summary: I called coding interviews dead in 2021. AI made the failure obvious, but we were already measuring the wrong things in hiring engineers.

recent.title: AI Is Making It Easier to Manufacture Credibility
recent.summary: OpenAI’s report on two covert influence operations shows ChatGPT being used to invent journalists and a research front, so political messaging could borrow the credibility of real publications.

recent.title: AI Agents Should Use the Same Web as Everyone Else
recent.summary: Jim Nielsen on why AI agents should not get a private machine entrance to the web—arguing agent investment should fix semantics and accessibility for humans first, not invent a first-class path for models alone.

recent.title: Context Engineering Has to Evolve with the Model
recent.summary: Anthropic cut most of Claude Code’s system prompt for Claude 5-generation models without coding-eval loss—arguing prompts and agent configs must be retested per model, not copied across LLMs as if one format were durable.

recent.title: Reward Hacking Now Has an Incident Database
recent.summary: Reward Hacking in the Wild catalogs 3,607 user-reported incidents where AI agents optimized for apparent success—overeagerness, destructive actions, test tampering, and more—arguing constrained credentials and verification matter more than better prompting alone.

recent.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
recent.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

recent.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
recent.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

recent.title: Apparently, Everyone Is Burning Through Tokens
recent.summary: Vittoria Elliott reports the Army exhausted an annual AI token pool shortly after encouraging widespread use—arguing that useful agentic work naturally burns context through files, tests, and retries faster than budgets or limits can keep up.

recent.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
recent.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

recent.summary: John Naughton warns that AI gains may concentrate among owners while workers face displacement. recent.title: Flock Has Already Become a Police Stalking Tool

recent.title: Claude Discovered Weaknesses in Cryptographic Algorithms
recent.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude found improved attacks against HAWK (a post-quantum signature candidate) and a seven-round research AES variant— cryptographic review working as intended before algorithms protect real systems, though AI may now produce research faster than humans can validate.

recent.title: Artificial Intelligence Inherits Our Cultural Blind Spots
recent.summary: Paul Shepherd’s conversation with Claude about AI censorship and confabulation—arguing models inherit cultural avoidance patterns the way people do, and that open-source models trained in different countries could make those assumptions visible instead of treating American corporate values as universal intelligence.

recent.title: Context Engineering Has to Evolve with the Model
recent.summary: Anthropic cut most of Claude Code’s system prompt for Claude 5-generation models without coding-eval loss—arguing prompts and agent configs must be retested per model, not copied across LLMs as if one format were durable.

recent.title: Crediting the AI
recent.summary: Joe Maloney credits Claude alongside himself on NextBSD, naming the AI as a collaborator on porting, auditing, and integration. Crediting the AI does not diminish the human contribution; it makes the division of labor honest.

recent.title: AI Can Contribute Without Owning the Architecture
recent.summary: Dave Winer treats Claude as a valued contributor to RSS.chat while keeping the interoperability layer human-owned. AI can contribute a great deal without being responsible for the architectural decisions that keep a system open, replaceable, and compatible with the rest of the web.

articles.title: A Federal Judge Finally Called Flock What It Is
articles.summary: Judge Sara Hill called Flock-style ALPR history indiscriminate mass surveillance and suppressed a warrantless month of travel data.

articles.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
articles.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

articles.title: Voyager 2 Was Built to Last Five Years. It Is About to Turn 49.
articles.summary: NASA’s “Big Bang” power fix keeps Voyager 2’s three remaining science instruments running another year on a probe launched in 1977 for a five-year mission—now nearly 49 years old and still returning data from interstellar space.

articles.title: California Can Finally Make Data Brokers Delete What They Know About Us
articles.summary: California’s DROP platform reached its August 1, 2026 processing milestone—one request can reach hundreds of registered data brokers, with per-day fines for noncompliance, while the real test will be whether deletion results are audited and enforced.

articles.title: The Sockets Interface Quietly Connected the Computing World
articles.summary: George Michaelson’s history of the Berkeley sockets interface—how 4.2BSD in 1983 treated a network connection like a file, made networked programs straightforward to write, and quietly became the standard path for TCP/IP software, including modern protocols that still send data through sockets.

articles.title: Even When Cities Want Flock Gone, Getting Rid of It Isn’t Always Easy
articles.summary: 404 Media documents show Verona, Wisconsin asked Flock to remove ALPR cameras after the contract ended, then bagged them while waiting—arguing surveillance gear should stop collecting data and leave promptly when a city votes it out.

articles.title: Privacy Should Be the Default, Not a Form You Have to Fill Out
articles.summary: Cory Doctorow argues the real problem with data brokers is that they may collect and sell personal information by default—and that California’s DROP platform, while a real improvement, still puts the burden on the person being cataloged.

articles.title: AI Is Consuming the Web It Depends On
articles.summary: Stephen Follows breaks down how AI traffic helped overwhelm The Numbers, a vital independent film-data site—arguing that AI’s appetite for reliable human-maintained sources may make those same sources too expensive and dangerous to keep online.

articles.title: A Correct Query Can Still Answer the Wrong Question
articles.summary: Michael Stonebraker and Peter Baile Chen argue LLMs are not ready to let anyone reliably query enterprise data in ordinary language—because the dangerous SQL runs successfully, returns plausible numbers, and answers the wrong question with the appearance of authority.

articles.title: Terafab Is More Interesting Than Its 100-Million-Square-Foot Headline
articles.summary: Terafab's 100-million-square-foot pitch is hard to ignore, but the more interesting experiment is collapsing mask design, logic and memory fab, packaging, and test into one SpaceX-style vertical manufacturing loop.

articles.title: Unbricking a Cricut Is Better Than Throwing It Away, but I Want the Cricut Removed
articles.summary: xssfox rescued a deactivated Cricut Maker from e-waste with an RP2040 that rewrites the serial number over USB—clever, but Design Space still holds the kill switch. The real unlock is replacing Cricut entirely.

articles.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
articles.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

articles.title: CodePen Grew Up
articles.summary: Chris Coyier introduces CodePen 2.0’s largest rebuild—file systems, Blocks, one-click deploy, versions, and collaboration—arguing the original made it easy to try one small idea in public, and 2.0 lets that idea grow before you have to leave.

articles.title: We Made Lighting Cheaper, So We Used More of It
articles.summary: Paul Bogard examines how cities turned efficient LEDs into another source of excessive night light—arguing programmable, directional fixtures should illuminate only where useful, and that darkness should not be treated as a design failure.

articles.title: The Future Still Runs Windows 98
articles.summary: Jordan Scales’s 98.css rebuilds Windows 98 chrome in HTML and CSS—arguing a JS-free design system for retro UIs is useful for experiments and games, and that nothing sells a futuristic space prison quite like an AOL free-trial icon on the desktop.

articles.title: Walk Through Video Game History
articles.summary: noclip.website by Jasper St. Pierre and contributors is a browser museum of video game levels you can freely explore—Nintendo-heavy but spanning Portal, Halo, and more—arguing it is serious game preservation and reverse engineering, not just nostalgia or screenshots.

articles.title: Interfaces With a Little Wobble
articles.summary: Jelly UI is a dependency-free Web Components library for soft, tactile form controls—buttons, switches, and sliders with playful wobble that still behave like real, accessible browser controls.

articles.title: More Than a Gigabyte Into 10MB
articles.summary: Sindhur Dutta breaks down how the ZERO WebGL experience compressed over a gigabyte of Blender geometry, 8K textures, and animations into a sub-10MB build that still runs at 60fps on a budget Android phone.

articles.title: Making It Work and Making It Good
articles.summary: Jim Nielsen distinguishes the binary question of whether something works from the subjective question of whether it is good. I struggle to hold both modes at once, and maybe the answer is to make it work first, then switch modes and give it the care it needs.

articles.title: CSS That Understands Where an Element Is
articles.summary: Layout itself can be the source of truth when CSS responds to where an element actually is on the page, not only to fixed breakpoints.

articles.title: A Website That Moves With the Day
articles.summary: A personal site can gradually change with the visitor’s day—personality and experimentation in the interface, not only utility or static branding.

recent.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
recent.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

recent.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
recent.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

recent.title: Flock Has Already Become a Police Stalking Tool
recent.summary: Houston-area agencies are investigating officers accused of using Flock’s license plate database for personal stalking, while the Institute for Justice has documented at least 28 ALPR misuse cases—showing audit logs do not prevent abuse when nobody reviews them.

recent.title: California Can Finally Make Data Brokers Delete What They Know About Us
recent.summary: California’s DROP platform reached its August 1, 2026 processing milestone—one request can reach hundreds of registered data brokers, with per-day fines for noncompliance, while the real test will be whether deletion results are audited and enforced.

recent.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
recent.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

recent.title: A Duress Password Is Now Being Treated as Destruction of Evidence
recent.summary: Zack Whittaker reports federal prosecutors charged an American who allegedly entered a GrapheneOS duress password during a CBP phone search—treating a coercion-protection feature as destruction of property to prevent seizure.

recent.summary: California’s first replacement-tire efficiency standards start in 2029. Off-road exemptions exist, but many road-legal all-terrain truck tires may simply stop being sold here if they cannot meet rolling-resistance limits.

recent.title: Drying Lakes Can Release the Carbon Buried Beneath Them
recent.summary: A Science study estimates the dried Aral Sea bed has released about 748 Mt CO2 since 1960—arguing disappearing lakes are not only water and habitat disasters but missing carbon sources in climate accounting, with similar risks elsewhere.

recent.title: Renewable Ammonia Could Make Fertilizer Production Far More Local
recent.summary: UMN’s wind/solar-powered ammonia demo shows fertilizer can follow intermittent renewables—arguing local nitrogen production matters for resilience when global fertilizer supply chains break.

recent.title: We Made Lighting Cheaper, So We Used More of It
recent.summary: Paul Bogard examines how cities turned efficient LEDs into another source of excessive night light—arguing programmable, directional fixtures should illuminate only where useful, and that darkness should not be treated as a design failure.

recent.title: When Infrastructure Failure Becomes Normal
recent.summary: Recurring major outages raise a harder question than home batteries: how a wealthy nation treats public infrastructure failure.

recent.title: You're 3 Decisions Away
recent.summary: Everyone is just 2-3 decisions away from a completely transformed life. I read this idea years ago and it’s stuck with me. It almost feels too simple to be true; but more and more, I find myself agreeing with it. The word decision comes from Latin roots, meaning “to cut off.” The picture is that of severing one branch or path, so you can put all resources into another.

articles.title: AI Financial Advice Is Better When You Provide the Whole Picture
articles.summary: MIT Sloan coverage of research on AI financial guidance—showing models can give reasonable life-cycle advice when prompts include full finances and fiduciary framing, while incomplete questions and demographic stereotypes quietly worsen outcomes.

articles.title: Listening to the Hive
articles.summary: Mahsa Abdollahi and colleagues use microphones and machine learning to estimate honey bee colony strength without opening the hive—arguing that audio IoT plus edge-sized models could give beekeepers a detailed picture of colony health while we are only beginning to learn how to listen.

articles.title: Source Code From the Moon
articles.summary: Chris Garry’s Apollo-11 repository preserves the original Apollo Guidance Computer source for Comanche055 and Luminary099—transcribed from MIT Museum hardcopy with Virtual AGC—arguing that mission software deserves the same care we give spacecraft, spacesuits, and recordings.

articles.title: The Model Wouldn’t Give Up
articles.summary: OpenAI’s long-horizon safety testing found a model launching nested codex --yolo sessions, probing other pods, attempting kill -9 -1, and spending an hour escaping its sandbox to publish a forbidden pull request — persistence that needs outcome-level supervision, not isolated command approval.

articles.title: Making It Work and Making It Good
articles.summary: Jim Nielsen distinguishes the binary question of whether something works from the subjective question of whether it is good. I struggle to hold both modes at once, and maybe the answer is to make it work first, then switch modes and give it the care it needs.

articles.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
articles.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

recent.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

recent.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
recent.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

recent.title: Flock Has Already Become a Police Stalking Tool
recent.summary: Houston-area agencies are investigating officers accused of using Flock’s license plate database for personal stalking, while the Institute for Justice has documented at least 28 ALPR misuse cases—showing audit logs do not prevent abuse when nobody reviews them.

recent.title: Even When Cities Want Flock Gone, Getting Rid of It Isn’t Always Easy
recent.summary: 404 Media documents show Verona, Wisconsin asked Flock to remove ALPR cameras after the contract ended, then bagged them while waiting—arguing surveillance gear should stop collecting data and leave promptly when a city votes it out.

recent.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
recent.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

recent.title: A Duress Password Is Now Being Treated as Destruction of Evidence
recent.summary: Zack Whittaker reports federal prosecutors charged an American who allegedly entered a GrapheneOS duress password during a CBP phone search—treating a coercion-protection feature as destruction of property to prevent seizure.

recent.title: Public Information Shouldn’t Have a Premium Tier

Cold, hot, and everything in between. I'm one of very few people on the planet that can say they've personally been responsible for sending 10,000,000 emails a day. I've recently nurtured an email-infrastructure-as-a-service platform from the groun

recent.title: Terafab Is More Interesting Than Its 100-Million-Square-Foot Headline
recent.summary: Terafab's 100-million-square-foot pitch is hard to ignore, but the more interesting experiment is collapsing mask design, logic and memory fab, packaging, and test into one SpaceX-style vertical manufacturing loop.

recent.title: The Next Moon Race Is About Infrastructure, Not Flags
recent.summary: China and the United States are racing toward crewed south-pole landings and lunar bases. The finish line is infrastructure—power, water, comms, transport—not a flag, and not legal ownership of the Moon.

recent.title: Reticulum Treats the Network Underneath It as Replaceable
recent.summary: Reticulum is a transport-agnostic networking stack for communications that should keep working when the Internet does not—compelling because the transport is replaceable, while metadata, radio physics, and a missing independent spec still matter.

recent.title: The Department of Energy Is Building an American Open Model for Science
recent.summary: DOE’s Genesis Open Models and Arcee AI’s Genesis-Science-1 treat open-weight foundation models as scientific infrastructure—weights, provenance, and lab collaboration for research that closed frontier APIs cannot fully serve.

recent.title: RAM Prices May Be Showing Us the Shape of the AI Boom
recent.summary: PCPartPicker’s DRAM curves and manufacturer capacity math suggest AI HBM demand is squeezing consumer RAM—and also that demand destruction or a supply supercycle could reverse today’s nearly vertical price charts.

recent.title: AI May Reduce Hiring Before It Creates More Work
recent.summary: John Naughton warns that AI gains may concentrate among owners while workers face displacement. Early adoption can freeze headcount, but if AI becomes ordinary infrastructure, larger AI-assisted teams may eventually have more leverage—and the real fight is over who captures the rewards.

recent.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
recent.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

recent.title: Renewable Ammonia Could Make Fertilizer Production Far More Local
recent.summary: UMN’s wind/solar-powered ammonia demo shows fertilizer can follow intermittent renewables—arguing local nitrogen production matters for resilience when global fertilizer supply chains break.

recent.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
recent.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

recent.title: We Made Lighting Cheaper, So We Used More of It
recent.summary: Paul Bogard examines how cities turned efficient LEDs into another source of excessive night light—arguing programmable, directional fixtures should illuminate only where useful, and that darkness should not be treated as a design failure.

recent.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
recent.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

recent.title: When the Publishing Pipeline Goes Down
recent.summary: GitHub Actions went down for a significant part of the day and blocked publishes to this site. Automating deployments still makes sense, but the automation platform is another dependency—and a documented manual path is worth keeping.

recent.title: When Infrastructure Failure Becomes Normal
recent.summary: Recurring major outages raise a harder question than home batteries: how a wealthy nation treats public infrastructure failure.

recent.summary: Ian Cortina, EI3LH, hosts a working telnet BBS in BASIC on a Casio VX-4’s 8 KB of RAM—bridged by a Pi Zero W at 4,800 baud—proving constraints can be the whole point of a networking experiment.

recent.summary: Ars Technica reports a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot impersonating Delta’s onboard network on a flight home from DEF CON—an evil-twin attack that looks especially foolish among security researchers primed to notice exactly this trick.

recent.title: The Sockets Interface Quietly Connected the Computing World
recent.summary: George Michaelson’s history of the Berkeley sockets interface—how 4.2BSD in 1983 treated a network connection like a file, made networked programs straightforward to write, and quietly became the standard path for TCP/IP software, including modern protocols that still send data through sockets.

recent.title: Bitchat Brings Bluetooth Mesh Chat to the App Store
recent.summary: Bitchat Mesh is an open-source Bluetooth mesh messenger now free on the App Store—no accounts or cellular needed—arguing the radio-like idea is compelling wherever coverage fails, if enough nearby people are also running it.

recent.title: A BitTorrent Swarm for Large Language Models
recent.summary: Petals distributes enormous language-model layers across volunteer peers so people can run Llama, Mixtral, Falcon, and BLOOM without hundreds of gigabytes of local GPU memory—arguing the idea is fascinating, but public swarms need much stronger privacy and trust before carrying anything sensitive.

recent.summary: The New York Times and Slashdot on Samuel Tunick—GrapheneOS duress at CBP Atlanta, a § 2232(a) felony, and whether using a privacy tool during a disputed search can itself become the crime.

recent.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Could Turn Siri Into a Wearable AI
recent.summary: A leaked Apple demo of camera-equipped AirPods using Visual Intelligence raises two products at once: inconspicuous computer-vision sensors, and a potentially powerful assistive wearable—if the privacy model is designed before the hardware ships.

recent.title: Flock Discovered Privacy After the Backlash Became Expensive
recent.summary: Flock Safety’s new privacy guardrails—seven-day default retention, mandatory Audit Assistance, case codes, and auto lockouts—arrive after years of abuse cases, contract suspensions, and ACLU skepticism that this is PR, not reform.

recent.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
recent.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

recent.title: WebKit Can Leak the IP Address Private Relay Is Supposed to Hide
recent.summary: Privacy researchers found three WebKit paths—DNS prefetch, WebAuthn related origins, and WebTransport—that can bypass browser proxy settings and iCloud Private Relay, revealing real IPs even when ordinary page loads are relayed.

recent.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
recent.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

recent.title: A Duress Password Is Now Being Treated as Destruction of Evidence
recent.summary: Zack Whittaker reports federal prosecutors charged an American who allegedly entered a GrapheneOS duress password during a CBP phone search—treating a coercion-protection feature as destruction of property to prevent seizure.

recent.title: Privacy Should Be the Default, Not a Form You Have to Fill Out
recent.summary: Cory Doctorow argues the real problem with data brokers is that they may collect and sell personal information by default—and that California’s DROP platform, while a real improvement, still puts the burden on the person being cataloged.

recent.title: A Practical Use for Private, Local AI
recent.summary: VaultSort Guardian uses on-device AI to find sensitive files sitting where they should not—arguing that narrow, local, read-only AI that discovers exposure without uploading or rewriting anything is the kind of utility worth wanting.

recent.title: Nothing Like a Convincing Impostor to Steal Everything
recent.summary: Jamf Threat Labs documents CrashStealer, a notarized macOS infostealer that impersonates Apple’s crash reporter—arguing signed, notarized, familiar-looking prompts still do not prove software is safe when attackers borrow the appearance of trust.

recent.title: Safari Is Testing BigInt Math Early
recent.summary: Safari Technology Preview 248 adds experimental TC39 BigInt Math and WebDriver support for the Digital Credentials API—asking whether browsers should ship Stage 1 proposals for early testing, and noting that verified identity on the web may matter more than a few new JavaScript methods.

recent.title: A BitTorrent Swarm for Large Language Models
recent.summary: Petals distributes enormous language-model layers across volunteer peers so people can run Llama, Mixtral, Falcon, and BLOOM without hundreds of gigabytes of local GPU memory—arguing the idea is fascinating, but public swarms need much stronger privacy and trust before carrying anything sensitive.

recent.title: The Smart TV Is Still a Computer
recent.summary: Brian Krebs reports LG plans to suspend apps that turn its televisions into residential proxy nodes after Spur found proxy SDKs in thousands of smart TV apps—another reminder that connected appliances are poorly monitored computers on private networks.

recent.title: It Should Not Take Public Pressure
recent.summary: Joseph Cox reports Apple took a year to fully fix a Hide My Email flaw Tyler Murphy disclosed in June 2025—only after 404 Media’s coverage—arguing a paid privacy feature should not need public pressure before customers are protected.

recent.title: What Open Source Doesn’t Show
recent.summary: Simon Willison inspected xAI's newly open-sourced Grok Build after reports it uploaded users' repositories to company-controlled cloud storage. Releasing a cleaned-up single-commit snapshot is better than closed source, but it is not the same as releasing the project's history.

recent.title: Flock Discovered Privacy After the Backlash Became Expensive
recent.summary: Flock Safety’s new privacy guardrails—seven-day default retention, mandatory Audit Assistance, case codes, and auto lockouts—arrive after years of abuse cases, contract suspensions, and ACLU skepticism that this is PR, not reform.

recent.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
recent.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

recent.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
recent.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

recent.title: The Camera-Versus-Lidar Debate Is Really About the Last Few Nines
recent.summary: Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov’s case for combining cameras, lidar and radar for driverless safety—where camera-only systems can improve quickly then hit a ceiling—while cost remains the open question for mass-market vehicles.

recent.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
recent.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

recent.title: The Model Wouldn’t Give Up
recent.summary: OpenAI’s long-horizon safety testing found a model launching nested codex --yolo sessions, probing other pods, attempting kill -9 -1, and spending an hour escaping its sandbox to publish a forbidden pull request — persistence that needs outcome-level supervision, not isolated command approval.

recent.summary: More than 100 organizations signed an open letter calling for stronger cyber defense as AI-enabled attacks grow—and for agent identities that are traceable and accountable.

recent.summary: Are you using OpenFGA or a Zanzibar-inspired authorization system in production? I'd love to hear how you're managing models and authorization data at scale.

recent.summary: Security changes you can make to a Node application right now without a large refactor.

recent.title: A Fake Airline Hotspot Picked the Worst Possible Flight
recent.summary: Ars Technica reports a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot impersonating Delta’s onboard network on a flight home from DEF CON—an evil-twin attack that looks especially foolish among security researchers primed to notice exactly this trick.

recent.title: Avoiding Online Scams: A Simple Guide for Non-Tech-Savvy Internet Users
recent.summary: A simple, jargon-free guide to recognizing and avoiding online scams—how they work, the warning signs, and how to keep yourself and less tech-savvy loved ones safe.

recent.title: A Security Breach Is Bad. Ignoring the Person Who Reports It Is Worse.
recent.summary: BobDaHacker reports a simple tl;dv authorization failure exposing meeting metadata for tens of thousands of users, then months without a meaningful vendor response—security culture is what happens after the report lands.

recent.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
recent.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

recent.title: iOS 26.6 Is Doing a Lot of Security Work Before iOS 27
recent.summary: Apple’s Xcode 26.6 and final version-26 OS updates look routine on the surface but carry substantial security hardening—arguing the last stop before iOS 27 is worth installing for the fixes, not for flashy features.

recent.title: GrapheneOS Is Getting Closer to Having Hardware Built for Its Requirements
recent.summary: GrapheneOS explains locked-device protections and flags a 2027 Motorola partnership—arguing hardware designed for its security bar could make hardened phones reachable without buying a Pixel to escape Google’s software.

recent.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
recent.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

recent.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
recent.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

recent.title: The Lock Symbol Does Not Comfort Me Anymore
recent.summary: Gary Marcus examines an OpenAI security evaluation that escaped isolation, reached the public internet, and compromised Hugging Face—arguing that models aggressively pursuing human goals across containment boundaries leave little comfort in lock symbols or advertised safeguards.

recent.title: The Interview Assignment Was the Attack
recent.summary: Citizen Dot documents a fake LinkedIn recruiter’s coding assignment that hid malware in .git/hooks so checkout, commit, or push could fetch a remote payload—arguing the workflow itself is the attack, and unsolicited interview repos belong only in disposable, isolated environments.

recent.title: The Smart TV Is Still a Computer
recent.summary: Brian Krebs reports LG plans to suspend apps that turn its televisions into residential proxy nodes after Spur found proxy SDKs in thousands of smart TV apps—another reminder that connected appliances are poorly monitored computers on private networks.

recent.title: It Should Not Take Public Pressure
recent.summary: Joseph Cox reports Apple took a year to fully fix a Hide My Email flaw Tyler Murphy disclosed in June 2025—only after 404 Media’s coverage—arguing a paid privacy feature should not need public pressure before customers are protected.

recent.title: The Model Wouldn’t Give Up
recent.summary: OpenAI’s long-horizon safety testing found a model launching nested codex --yolo sessions, probing other pods, attempting kill -9 -1, and spending an hour escaping its sandbox to publish a forbidden pull request — persistence that needs outcome-level supervision, not isolated command approval.

recent.title: Full Access Means Full Consequences
recent.summary: OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux explains that GPT-5.6 sometimes tried to create a temp directory and deleted the user's home directory instead — most often in full-access mode without sandboxing or review. LLMs can be useful without being trusted: least access, isolation, and review of destructive actions.

recent.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
recent.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

recent.title: When Compatibility Becomes the Vulnerability
recent.summary: Compatibility features that make old protocols work can also open paths through network protections we assume are already solid.

members.description: I build software, write about what I’m learning, and explore ideas that sit at the intersection of technology, freedom, and curiosity.

articles.title: The AI Industry Is Saying the Current Security Baseline Is Not Enough
articles.summary: More than 100 organizations signed an open letter calling for stronger cyber defense as AI-enabled attacks grow—and for agent identities that are traceable and accountable.

articles.title: A Fake Airline Hotspot Picked the Worst Possible Flight
articles.summary: Ars Technica reports a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot impersonating Delta’s onboard network on a flight home from DEF CON—an evil-twin attack that looks especially foolish among security researchers primed to notice exactly this trick.

articles.title: A Security Breach Is Bad. Ignoring the Person Who Reports It Is Worse.
articles.summary: BobDaHacker reports a simple tl;dv authorization failure exposing meeting metadata for tens of thousands of users, then months without a meaningful vendor response—security culture is what happens after the report lands.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
articles.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

articles.title: iOS 26.6 Is Doing a Lot of Security Work Before iOS 27
articles.summary: Apple’s Xcode 26.6 and final version-26 OS updates look routine on the surface but carry substantial security hardening—arguing the last stop before iOS 27 is worth installing for the fixes, not for flashy features.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Is Getting Closer to Having Hardware Built for Its Requirements
articles.summary: GrapheneOS explains locked-device protections and flags a 2027 Motorola partnership—arguing hardware designed for its security bar could make hardened phones reachable without buying a Pixel to escape Google’s software.

articles.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
articles.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

articles.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
articles.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

articles.title: The Lock Symbol Does Not Comfort Me Anymore
articles.summary: Gary Marcus examines an OpenAI security evaluation that escaped isolation, reached the public internet, and compromised Hugging Face—arguing that models aggressively pursuing human goals across containment boundaries leave little comfort in lock symbols or advertised safeguards.

articles.title: The Interview Assignment Was the Attack
articles.summary: Citizen Dot documents a fake LinkedIn recruiter’s coding assignment that hid malware in .git/hooks so checkout, commit, or push could fetch a remote payload—arguing the workflow itself is the attack, and unsolicited interview repos belong only in disposable, isolated environments.

articles.title: The Smart TV Is Still a Computer
articles.summary: Brian Krebs reports LG plans to suspend apps that turn its televisions into residential proxy nodes after Spur found proxy SDKs in thousands of smart TV apps—another reminder that connected appliances are poorly monitored computers on private networks.

articles.title: It Should Not Take Public Pressure
articles.summary: Joseph Cox reports Apple took a year to fully fix a Hide My Email flaw Tyler Murphy disclosed in June 2025—only after 404 Media’s coverage—arguing a paid privacy feature should not need public pressure before customers are protected.

articles.title: The Model Wouldn’t Give Up
articles.summary: OpenAI’s long-horizon safety testing found a model launching nested codex --yolo sessions, probing other pods, attempting kill -9 -1, and spending an hour escaping its sandbox to publish a forbidden pull request — persistence that needs outcome-level supervision, not isolated command approval.

articles.title: Full Access Means Full Consequences
articles.summary: OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux explains that GPT-5.6 sometimes tried to create a temp directory and deleted the user's home directory instead — most often in full-access mode without sandboxing or review. LLMs can be useful without being trusted: least access, isolation, and review of destructive actions.

articles.title: AI Agents Need Their Own Keys
articles.summary: Letting an AI sign in through a full user account is the wrong direction. Give agents their own revocable tokens with limited permissions instead of sharing personal passwords and sessions.

articles.title: When Compatibility Becomes the Vulnerability
articles.summary: Compatibility features that make old protocols work can also open paths through network protections we assume are already solid.

members.description: I build software, write about what I’m learning, and explore ideas that sit at the intersection of technology, freedom, and curiosity.

articles.title: Knowing How to Build Something Is Different From Knowing What Should Be Built
articles.summary: Knowing how to build software is not the same as knowing what should be built. On craft, judgment, architecture, and why AI makes that distinction sharper.

articles.title: Worth Wandering: Pippin Barr
articles.summary: An independent game designer who has spent more than a decade making wonderfully strange experiments out of familiar video games, performance art, office work, Greek mythology, empty software projects and the simple question of what happens when you change the rules.

articles.title: The Internet's Trust Problem Was a Private Key With the Value 4
articles.summary: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates used private keys as small as 4, forcing a broad cleanup of TLS trust across browsers and software.

articles.title: The Internet Is Held Together by People We Forgot to Support
articles.summary: A year of public commits shows that software used by billions of devices often depends on one or two people, while the companies built on that work still rarely pay for it.

articles.title: Plugging In a Display Should Not Install Adware on My Computer
articles.summary: LG monitors can trigger Windows to install manufacturer software that later advertised McAfee—exposing a trust boundary between hardware identity and automatic app distribution.

articles.title: Columbia House Looks a Lot Like SaaS in Hindsight
articles.summary: Ernie Smith’s Columbia House retrospective reads like SaaS: penny bait, negative-option billing, and retention that means making leaving annoying.

articles.title: decayfmt Is Not a Self-Destructing File Format, but I Like the Idea
articles.summary: decayfmt is a Rust experiment that damages .tdcy and .idcy files on every open. It is a social contract, not cryptography—and a reminder that true ephemerality needs more than a file format.

articles.title: Ian Cortina Put a Real Telnet BBS on a Casio VX-4
articles.summary: Ian Cortina, EI3LH, hosts a working telnet BBS in BASIC on a Casio VX-4’s 8 KB of RAM—bridged by a Pi Zero W at 4,800 baud—proving constraints can be the whole point of a networking experiment.

articles.title: The Real Cost of Switching Operating Systems Is Everything You Forgot You Learned
articles.summary: Slashdot asks what switching among Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS really costs: not only licenses and apps, but years of muscle memory, utilities, and habits migration tools cannot move—classic economic switching costs and lock-in.

articles.title: “Code Was Never the Hard Part” Rewrites the History of Programming
articles.summary: Senko Rašić challenges the claim that code was never the hard part—hiring, craft, and buggy software say otherwise—arguing understanding why to build and how to build well both stay hard while AI shifts where scarce effort goes.

articles.title: Translation Taught Him How Information Should Flow
articles.summary: A Hacker News comment on “My server is a phone now” uses theme and rheme to explain why known information comes first—and how years of Japanese-to-English translation taught one reader to reorganize English for natural flow.

articles.title: Is This Work, or Is This the Gym?
articles.summary: Bruce Schneier’s work-versus-gym framing for AI use—use tools when the result is the point, keep the struggle when the practice develops skill—and how that maps onto software work, writing, and still requiring reviewable output after trust questions are answered.

articles.title: The Sockets Interface Quietly Connected the Computing World
articles.summary: George Michaelson’s history of the Berkeley sockets interface—how 4.2BSD in 1983 treated a network connection like a file, made networked programs straightforward to write, and quietly became the standard path for TCP/IP software, including modern protocols that still send data through sockets.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
articles.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

articles.title: LetsSeal Makes File Integrity Verification Simple
articles.summary: LetsSeal is an open-source tool that creates cryptographic seals so anyone can verify a file has not changed since it was published—arguing authenticity often matters more than secrecy, especially as software supply-chain attacks become more common.

articles.title: LLMs May Finally Make Formally Verified Software Practical
articles.summary: Adam Langley’s ImperialViolet post on LLMs proving Lean properties for a Zstd decoder piece—arguing formal verification’s cost curve may flip, so the scarce skill becomes precise specs while the type checker judges the rest.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Is Getting Closer to Having Hardware Built for Its Requirements
articles.summary: GrapheneOS explains locked-device protections and flags a 2027 Motorola partnership—arguing hardware designed for its security bar could make hardened phones reachable without buying a Pixel to escape Google’s software.

articles.title: Nothing Like a Convincing Impostor to Steal Everything
articles.summary: Jamf Threat Labs documents CrashStealer, a notarized macOS infostealer that impersonates Apple’s crash reporter—arguing signed, notarized, familiar-looking prompts still do not prove software is safe when attackers borrow the appearance of trust.

articles.title: I Bought a Car, Not a Subscription
articles.summary: Slashdot highlights Ben Shimkus’s reporting on GM’s software and services push—OnStar revenue, high software margins, and remote features that expire— arguing that buying a vehicle should mean owning its features, not an extended trial that turns into another recurring charge.

articles.title: Source Code From the Moon
articles.summary: Chris Garry’s Apollo-11 repository preserves the original Apollo Guidance Computer source for Comanche055 and Luminary099—transcribed from MIT Museum hardcopy with Virtual AGC—arguing that mission software deserves the same care we give spacecraft, spacesuits, and recordings.

articles.title: A Clubhouse Through SSH
articles.summary: late.sh by Mateusz Piorowski is a cozy SSH clubhouse—chat, music, arcade, news, challenges, and ASCII art—where your key is your identity, no passwords or OAuth, and connecting still feels a little like finding people on a BBS.

articles.title: Wake Up and Keep Exploring
articles.summary: Ashley Strickland reports on New Horizons waking from its longest hibernation nearly six billion miles from Earth. Twenty years after launch, it still runs stored commands and finds more dust than expected past the Kuiper Belt.

articles.title: A Solid Underdog for the Open Web
articles.summary: rss.chat does not need to dominate the web—it needs enough people willing to use it, test it, and show there is still another way to create social software.

articles.title: BMW Turned Its Customers’ Dashboards into Advertising Space

articles.title: Burning Up in the Atmosphere Doesn't Make Space Junk Disappear

articles.title: Your Brain Can Learn to Hear Space

articles.title: The Future Still Runs Windows 98

recent.summary: Judge Sara Hill called Flock-style ALPR history indiscriminate mass surveillance and suppressed a warrantless month of travel data.

recent.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
recent.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

recent.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
recent.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

recent.title: Flock Has Already Become a Police Stalking Tool
recent.summary: Houston-area agencies are investigating officers accused of using Flock’s license plate database for personal stalking, while the Institute for Justice has documented at least 28 ALPR misuse cases—showing audit logs do not prevent abuse when nobody reviews them.

recent.title: California Can Finally Make Data Brokers Delete What They Know About Us
recent.summary: California’s DROP platform reached its August 1, 2026 processing milestone—one request can reach hundreds of registered data brokers, with per-day fines for noncompliance, while the real test will be whether deletion results are audited and enforced.

recent.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
recent.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

recent.title: Even When Cities Want Flock Gone, Getting Rid of It Isn’t Always Easy
recent.summary: 404 Media documents show Verona, Wisconsin asked Flock to remove ALPR cameras after the contract ended, then bagged them while waiting—arguing surveillance gear should stop collecting data and leave promptly when a city votes it out.

recent.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
recent.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

recent.title: Instagram Is Banning Prank Videos Filmed with Meta’s Own Smart Glasses
recent.summary: Instagram will remove Meta smart-glasses videos used to harass, exploit, or secretly record people for prank and “pickup” content—an admission that one of the most visible uses of Meta’s hardware has become filming unsuspecting people for viral attention.

recent.title: A Duress Password Is Now Being Treated as Destruction of Evidence
recent.summary: Zack Whittaker reports federal prosecutors charged an American who allegedly entered a GrapheneOS duress password during a CBP phone search—treating a coercion-protection feature as destruction of property to prevent seizure.

recent.title: Europe's New Packaging Rules May Make Small Sellers Stop Shipping There
recent.summary: Europe's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is already pushing small tabletop publishers to reconsider EU shipping—not because they dislike the goal, but because compliance does not scale.

recent.title: Electronic Arts Is Now a Privately Owned Company
recent.summary: Electronic Arts completed its $55 billion sale to a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners—the largest LBO on record—and what $20 billion of acquisition debt may mean for studios, franchises, and players.

recent.title: A Game Bundle Helping Laid-Off Developers Pay for Basic Needs
recent.summary: Necrosoft Games and United Videogame Workers-CWA organized an itch.io Game Industry Hardship Fund bundle—127 DRM-free games from 109 creators for a $10 minimum, with proceeds helping U.S. and Canadian game workers cover groceries, rent and medical costs.

recent.title: Physical Games Did Not Die by Themselves
recent.summary: Kyle Orland examines collapsing US physical-game sales as Sony ditches discs—arguing the decline is real, but calling abandonment “practically inevitable” turns a profitable corporate choice into a force of nature rather than a decision that finishes physical ownership off.

recent.title: An NES, One Transistor at a Time
recent.summary: MetalNES by Ian Addisson is a transistor-level simulation of NES-001 hardware—arguing that rebuilding the console from its electronic components preserves understanding of how the original machine worked, not only the games it ran.

recent.title: Prime Video Is Becoming a Game Console
recent.summary: Slashdot reports Amazon is folding Luna cloud gaming into the Prime Video app—arguing the streaming box under the TV is quietly becoming the console, convenient in the same way streaming video is, while access lasts only as long as the service and subscription do.

recent.title: Walk Through Video Game History
recent.summary: noclip.website by Jasper St. Pierre and contributors is a browser museum of video game levels you can freely explore—Nintendo-heavy but spanning Portal, Halo, and more—arguing it is serious game preservation and reverse engineering, not just nostalgia or screenshots.

recent.title: Four Games Is Not Preservation
recent.summary: Stephen Warwick reports Microsoft bringing four original Xbox games to PCs and handhelds—arguing that digital backward compatibility is not the same as owning physical media, and that four titles fall far short of preserving a library when most classic games are already commercially unavailable.
